title: Volume Integrals in Mechanics
short_intro: Volume integrals mathematically accumulate scalar or vector fields over a bounded three-dimensional region in space. In mechanics, they are foundational for evaluating continuous mass distributions, gravitational potentials, and inertial properties.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Evaluation of simple volume integrals in Cartesian coordinates for mass, volume, and uniform density bodies.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Transformation of volume integrals to cylindrical and spherical polar coordinates for calculating moments of inertia, center of mass, and gravitational self-potential for non-uniform bodies.

prerequisites: Vector calculus and triple integration techniques
Coordinate transformations (Cartesian to cylindrical and spherical)
Definition of density, mass, and center of mass

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Meaning
bullets: A volume integral integrates a continuous scalar function f(x, y, z) over a defined region V in three-dimensional space.
Represented mathematically as triply nested integrals with the differential volume element dV = dx dy dz in Cartesian coordinates.
Physically, when the integrand represents mass density rho(x, y, z), the volume integral yields the total mass of the continuous body.

concept_notes.heading: Differential Volume Elements in Curvilinear Coordinates
bullets: In cylindrical coordinates (r, theta, z), the volume element is given by dV = r dr dtheta dz, arising from the Jacobian determinant of the coordinate transformation.
In spherical polar coordinates (r, theta, phi), the volume element is dV = r² sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi, where theta is the polar angle and phi is the azimuth.
Choosing the appropriate coordinate system exploits the spatial symmetry of mechanical systems, simplifying calculations for central forces and rotational dynamics.

concept_notes.heading: Application to Center of Mass
bullets: The position vector of the center of mass R_cm of a continuous body is defined via the volume integral of position weighted by density: R_cm = (1/M) int r rho(r) dV.
Total mass M is evaluated using the zeroth-order volume integral of the density function over the entire volume V.
Symmetry arguments simplify these integrals; if a body possesses a plane of symmetry, the center of mass lies directly on that plane.

concept_notes.heading: Application to Moment of Inertia and Gravitational Potential
bullets: Moments of inertia for continuous rigid bodies are calculated by integrating the square of the perpendicular distance from an axis multiplied by density over the volume.
Gravitational potential V(r) at an external point due to a continuous mass distribution is evaluated by integrating over the source volume elements dV.
These integrals directly link macroscopic inertial properties to microscopic mass distributions, crucial for analyzing angular momentum and central force motion.

derivations.title: Mass of a Solid Sphere of Non-Uniform Density
derivations.conditions: Sphere of radius R with density varying radially as rho(r) = rho_0 (1 - r/R)
steps: Write the volume integral for mass in spherical polar coordinates: M = int_V rho(r) dV.
Substitute the volume element dV = r² sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi and the given density function.
Integrate over the angular variables: int_0^{2pi} dphi = 2pi and int_0^{pi} sin(theta) dtheta = 2.
Evaluate the radial integral: M = 2pi * 2 * int_0^R rho_0 (1 - r/R) r² dr.
Perform the integration: M = 4pi rho_0 [ R^3/3 - R^3/4 ] = (pi rho_0 R^3)/3.

derivations.title: Center of Mass of a Hemispherical Shell of Uniform Density
derivations.conditions: Solid hemisphere of uniform density rho and radius R
steps: Use cylindrical or spherical coordinates due to axial symmetry; by symmetry, X_cm = Y_cm = 0.
Set up the integral for the Z-coordinate of the center of mass: Z_cm = (1/M) int_V z rho dV.
In spherical coordinates, z = r cos(theta), and dV = r² sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi.
Integrate over V where r ranges from 0 to R, theta from 0 to pi/2, and phi from 0 to 2pi.
Numerator yields rho * 2pi * int_0^R r^3 dr * int_0^{pi/2} cos(theta)sin(theta) dtheta = rho * 2pi * (R^4/4) * (1/2) = (pi rho R^4)/4.
Since M = (2/3)pi R^3 rho, divide the numerator by M.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spherical Coordinate Volume Element
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A differential volume wedge in spherical coordinates showing sides dr, r dtheta, and r sin(theta) dphi.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes how the product of the three orthogonal linear dimensions forms the spherical volume element dV = r^2 sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Helps students recall the origin of the r^2 sin(theta) Jacobian factor in triple integrals.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mass Element Integration in a Cylinder
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A cylindrical shell of radius r, thickness dr, and height h inside a solid cylinder.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the shell method for evaluating volume integrals in cylindrical coordinates where dV = 2pi r h dr for axisymmetric systems.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested in calculating moments of inertia of cylinders and disks.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Center of Mass Positioning for Non-Uniform Rod/Sphere
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sphere with a density gradient offset from the geometric center, indicating distinct geometric center vs center of mass.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that inhomogeneity shifts the center of mass away from the geometric center due to the weighted volume integral.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding non-uniform bodies in mechanics.

solved_numericals.question: Find the volume of a rectangular box bounded by planes x = 0, x = a, y = 0, y = b, and z = 0, z = c using a volume integral.
solution_steps: Set up the volume integral: V = int_0^c int_0^b int_0^a dx dy dz.
Integrate with respect to x: int_0^a dx = a.
Integrate with respect to y: int_0^b dy = b.
Integrate with respect to z: int_0^c dz = c.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the total mass of a solid sphere of radius R where the density varies with the distance r from the center according to rho(r) = rho_0 r.
solution_steps: Write the mass volume integral in spherical coordinates: M = int_0^{2pi} dphi int_0^{pi} sin(theta) dtheta int_0^R (rho_0 r) r^2 dr.
Evaluate the angular integrals: int_0^{2pi} dphi int_0^{pi} sin(theta) dtheta = 4pi.
Evaluate the radial integral: int_0^R rho_0 r^3 dr = rho_0 R^4 / 4.
Multiply the results: M = 4pi * (rho_0 R^4 / 4) = pi rho_0 R^4.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the moment of inertia about the Z-axis of a uniform cylinder of radius R, height h, and total mass M.
solution_steps: Use cylindrical coordinates where density is rho = M / (pi R^2 h).
Set up the moment of inertia integral: I_z = int_0^h dz int_0^{2pi} dtheta int_0^R (r^2) rho r dr.
Perform the radial integration: int_0^R r^3 dr = R^4 / 4.
Perform the angular and height integrations: int_0^{2pi} dtheta = 2pi and int_0^h dz = h.
Combine terms: I_z = (M / (pi R^2 h)) * (2pi) * h * (R^4 / 4) = (1/2) M R^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: The density function rho(x, y, z) must be continuous or piecewise continuous over the domain of integration.
The volume V must be bounded and measurable in R^3 for the Riemann volume integral to converge.
Relativistic mass variation is neglected; classical Newtonian mechanics and Euclidean geometry are assumed.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The volume element in spherical coordinates is simply dr dtheta dphi.
common_misconceptions.correct: The correct volume element is dV = r^2 sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi.
common_misconceptions.why: Failing to include the Jacobian determinant r^2 sin(theta) ignores the expansion of spherical volume shells with radius.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The center of mass always coincides with the geometric center of any object.
common_misconceptions.correct: The center of mass coincides with the geometric center only if the body is homogenous (uniform density) and possesses spatial symmetry.
common_misconceptions.why: Non-uniform density creates a position-dependent weighting in the volume integral, shifting the center of mass.

quick_revision: Volume integrals accumulate scalar fields over 3D space using dV.
Cartesian dV = dx dy dz, Cylindrical dV = r dr dtheta dz, Spherical dV = r^2 sin(theta) dr dtheta dphi.
Total mass is the volume integral of density: M = int rho dV.
Center of mass vector uses the first moment of mass divided by total mass.
